title: Cultural Humility vs. a Checklist
summary: Use cultural humility to question what you assume about people, and structured analysis to examine the decisions your team makes.
body:
Use cultural humility to question what you assume about people, and structured analysis to examine the decisions your team makes.

About this course

For DHS employees who develop policies, communicate with the public, deliver services, or support colleagues. This course connects individual inquiry with organizational analysis without assigning staff a score.

Recorded introduction

Cultural humility is curiosity that does not end. A checklist can still be the toolkit. This course holds both: do not reduce a people to a fact sheet, and do not refuse a form because it feels like a box. At Minnesota DHS the work in front of you still gets a who, data, and a date. Voluntary. This course does not assign a score.

Learning objectives

Distinguish what a cultural brief, a conversation, and an organizational checklist can each contribute to a DHS decision.

Explain how a team can follow a required process while remaining open to information that challenges its initial assumptions.

Develop a proportionate next step that identifies the concern, the responsible role, and the evidence needed to review the result.

Practice and reflection

Make and revise scenario-based decisions in the course without performance grading.

Use the activities to explain your reasoning and, if helpful, keep a private note about how you could apply it.

If useful, apply the ideas to a fictional example or an appropriate work question. Consult the relevant review process when considering an actual DHS decision.

Applying the learning

Choose a practice example or a work decision within your responsibility. Identify what the available information misses and how you could learn more before recommending a change.

Lesson sequence

Both are true

Learning about a community does not establish what an individual wants. Following a structured process does not remove the need for that conversation.

The limits of a fact sheet

A claim about “how Hmong families are” turns background information into a stereotype. Ask what matters to the particular person or family.

When a checklist is the right tool

An organizational checklist can direct attention to policies, resources, and service conditions. Its usefulness depends on the evidence behind each response.

Ask questions and set the review date

Turn a useful question into a responsible next step. Explain what can change, who can act, and how the person will learn what happened.

Job aid

Humility and Checklist Job Aid

Ask the person, examine the process, and follow through on what the evidence shows.

Community knowledge can improve your questions. It cannot determine an individual’s answer.

Refer to this aid when using the Cultural Humility vs. Checklist approach within a current DHS policy, service, or workplace review.

Keep individual preferences, organizational evidence, and formal responsibilities distinct as you decide what to do next.

When a right, complaint, labor process, safety duty, or Tribal consultation is involved, contact the person or area responsible and follow its required process.

For practice, choose a fictional example or an appropriate work issue. Describe affected roles or groups without names, identify what is known and uncertain, and recommend a proportionate next step to the responsible role. The evidence may support retaining a practice, revising it, or seeking further review.

Humility

Recognize that your perspective may not be complete.

Ask what matters to the person and check your interpretation of their answer.

Ask about communication needs and arrange appropriate support.

Use cultural briefs to prepare questions, not to predict a person’s preferences.

Checklist

Use the analysis process that applies to the decision before it is finalized.

Check how language-access arrangements work in practice, including how people learn about and use them.

Support checklist responses with organizational evidence and identify what remains uncertain.

Sources

NCCC checklists (Georgetown)

Georgetown’s National Center for Cultural Competence provides organizational self-assessment resources. Use the relevant tool’s guidance and examine supporting evidence; this course does not turn a checklist into a rating of a person.

(https://nccc.georgetown.edu/)

DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit (this hub)

Related program learning on the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. Check the current agency process and the scope of the decision rather than treating this course as the official procedure.

(/c/dhs-equity-analysis-toolkit)

Cultural broker as a role (this hub)

Related program learning on cultural brokering as a role. Use it to examine when contextual knowledge or communication support may help, while still asking the person about their own priorities.

(/c/cultural-broker-as-a-role)

title: Cultural humility in public service
summary: Cultural humility means learning what something means to the person and examining your own interpretation. It also means responding with thought to the influence your public-service role carries.
body:
Cultural humility means learning what something means to the person and examining your own interpretation. It also means responding with thought to the influence your public-service role carries.

About this course

For staff across DHS exploring cultural humility through original practice public-service and personal encounters. The foundational research arose in medical education; its self-examination, power and partnership concepts inform this course without becoming a universal legal procedure. Personal meanings are learned in context, not predicted from identity. This course does not assess a person’s intercultural orientation, determine benefits, authorize a process change or settle an allegation. Actual access, information, equity-analysis and role-specific duties remain separate. Private reflection with the example is valid; no personal disclosure or live records are required. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA. This foundations course focuses on cultural responsiveness with Minnesota communities. Builds shared language, awareness, and basic practices. No earlier modules are needed. Lessons can be opened in any order. Examples are practice. Keep reflection notes without identifying coworkers or members of the public. Use the applicable agency equity-analysis process for actual decisions; course routines are preparation and do not replace it. This course supports learning; formal employment, accommodation, civil-rights, eligibility, Tribal consultation and licensing decisions stay with the person or area responsible.

Recorded introduction

Cultural humility begins with the recognition that your first interpretation may leave something important unseen. Follow a practice conversation in which a prepared answer and an open question carry different learned meanings of respect. Explore how staff can understand those meanings, keep practical help available and examine the influence of their own role. Finish with a specific account of learning and unfinished questions rather than a claim of mastery. Work at your own pace and reflect privately if you prefer.

Learning objectives

Distinguish Nyra’s question from Luca’s interpretation of it.

Compare Luca’s and Tavi’s meanings the people describe of preparing an answer.

Distinguish a useful clarification from an unnecessary personal-information demand.

Identify practical ways Luca’s role influences the appointment conversation.

Distinguish a cultural-learning question from an actual responsibility or request.

Describe the specific meaning and behavior change in the example.

Practice and reflection

Make and reconsider scenario decisions without being assigned a score.

Use the knowledge checks and sorting activities to support a meaningful reflection or next practice.

Use the course job aid for personal understanding, a practice example, or an appropriate work task. Personal reflection can remain private and does not require entered notes or a work result.

Applying the learning

If useful, revisit the example or a suitable draft privately, at your own pace.

Lesson sequence

Examine the meaning you add

Separate the person’s words from the interpretation that your own learned experience supplies.

Understand different meanings of respectful preparation

Learn how a settled answer and a shared question can express personally learned responsibility in different ways.

Be curious without requiring disclosure

Ask a useful chosen question while keeping practical help available when personal sharing is declined.

Notice how your role shapes the encounter

Examine the influence of staff choices, explanations and routes without promising authority you do not have.

Keep required responsibilities clear

Respond through the actual access, employment and reporting processes while continuing appropriate learning.

Continue learning without claiming mastery

Recognize a particular interpretation change and keep unresolved conditions and missing feedback visible.

Job aid

Examine your interpretation, learn the person’s meaning and keep the actual responsibilities clear.

Use this aid to explore Cultural humility in public service through personal understanding, a practice example, or an appropriate work task. Private reflection does not need a work product or entered personal notes.

Humility is an ongoing practice rather than knowing every person in advance.

Understanding a supplied meaning does not require copying it or assigning it to a group.

A person’s practical help must not depend on sharing a personal history.

Actual responsibilities remain even when the conversation feels respectful.

Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.

Examine the first interpretation

What did the person actually say or do, and what meaning did you add?

Which personally learned experience makes your first reading feel natural? You may examine it privately without publishing a biography.

What other meaning has the person supplied? Do not infer one from identity, an accent, appearance or a presumed community rule.

Respond to the actual person

Ask a useful, chosen question about this situation. A person may decline personal sharing and still receive practical help.

Notice which options, words and routes your role controls. Explain actual choices and limits without promising an unapproved result.

Receive input without insisting that understanding requires agreement. Account for how it informed the question or decision, including an unchanged choice and its reasons.

Keep responsibilities separate

Cultural inquiry does not replace the actual access, consent, records, decision or required equity-analysis process.

For an employment accommodation request, promptly forward to the appropriate decision maker and simultaneously tell the requestor who that person is. Supervisors/managers must not request medical information or documentation; appropriate requests belong to the agency ADA Coordinator.

Managers and supervisors immediately report protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual agency procedures. Optional learning cannot postpone that response.

The consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff build their own capability. Support is available without a mandatory consultant approval to use resources.

Continue with an honest account

Name one interpretation clarified and how the response changed. Do not turn a specific encounter into a claim of cultural mastery or an assessment score.

Preserve the person’s feedback, unanswered conditions and missing information. Gratitude or silence does not establish every effect.

You can reflect privately, use the example, or consider an appropriate draft.

Continue your learning

Level: Foundations. Builds shared language, awareness, and basic practices. No earlier modules are needed.

Learning pathway: Community engagement.

Especially useful for: Division and section leaders; Managers and supervisors; Team leads and project leads; Policy and program staff; Data, research, and evaluation staff; Fiscal, rates, grants, and contract staff; Training, communications, and web content staff; Clinical and positive supports professionals; Operations and administrative staff; New employees (first year at DSD).

Lesson 6 connects this topic with related courses you can explore next.

Sources

Tervalon and Murray-García: cultural humility
The original 1998 article’s abstract describes ongoing self-examination, attention to power and nonpaternalistic partnership in medical education. Public-service scenarios here are instructional adaptations, not clinical findings or legal rules.
(https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10073197/)

Council of Europe: developing intercultural competence
Relevant sections explain individualized learned meanings, contextual interpretation, perspective-taking and self-understanding. No personal orientation or cultural group profile is inferred.
(https://rm.coe.int/16808ce258)

HHS: National CLAS Standards
A health and health-care blueprint for respectful, understandable and responsive services, organizational attention and meaningful partnership. Its standards do not by themselves decide every program’s legal requirement.
(https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/standards)

HHS: What is CLAS?
Describes respecting and responding to the whole individual and individual preferences, not assigning a uniform preference from identity.
(https://thinkculturalhealth.hhs.gov/clas/what-is-clas)

DHS Equity Policy
Actual staff responsibilities and required equity analysis remain distinct from optional reflection and the example.
(https://mn.gov/dhs/assets/equity-policy_tcm1053-646921.pdf)

MMB Policy 1433: ADA reasonable accommodation
Actual employment request recognition, forwarding and notice, authority, documentation and confidentiality requirements continue separately.
(https://mn.gov/mmb-stat/equal-opportunity/ada/1433-reasonable-accommodation.pdf)

title: Cultural Humility: Engaging Diverse Identities in Therapy
summary: Cultural Humility is a research-grounded guide for therapists and other helping professionals on how to work across difference. Its four authors are counseling psychologists who have led much of the research on humility in clinical settings. Their core claim is that cultural competence, understood as mastering facts about groups, is the wrong goal. What predicts good outcomes is a stance of openness, curiosity, and awareness of one's own limits. They call this stance cultural humility.
body:
Cultural Humility: Engaging Diverse Identities in Therapy
Joshua N. Hook, Don Davis, Jesse Owen, and Cirleen DeBlaere
Cultural Humility is a research-grounded guide for therapists and other helping professionals on how to work across difference. Its four authors are counseling psychologists who have led much of the research on humility in clinical settings. Their core claim is that cultural competence, understood as mastering facts about groups, is the wrong goal. What predicts good outcomes is a stance of openness, curiosity, and awareness of one's own limits. They call this stance cultural humility.
Cultural competence as mastery of facts about groups is an unreachable and sometimes harmful goal; cultural humility is a stance, not a credential.
Humility has an inward side (an accurate view of yourself) and an outward side (focusing on the other person with curiosity).
In the authors' research, client ratings of a therapist's cultural humility predict the working alliance and outcomes.
The multicultural orientation framework combines humility, cultural opportunities, and cultural comfort.
Cultural opportunities are moments when identity comes to the front; noticing and exploring them is a skill people can learn.
Anxiety reduces curiosity, so building comfort with talks about culture is part of the work.
Missed opportunities and microaggressions will happen; repairing them without defensiveness is a core skill.
Intersectionality matters: no single identity explains a person.
Feedback from clients, peers, and supervisors is essential because people judge their own humility poorly.
Organizations and training programs can either support or undermine humility through their structures and incentives.
This book gives human-services organizations a research-backed alternative to one-off cultural competence trainings. Supervisors can use the cultural-opportunities idea in case reviews. They can ask staff where identity came up in an interaction and what they did with it. Training designers can build comfort through role-play and reflective practice instead of lectures. HR can frame humility as an expectation for growth, not a compliance checkbox. The main caveat is that most of the evidence comes from psychotherapy and relies on client self-report. Applying it to case management, benefits work, or policy work takes some adaptation. Some critics also argue that a personal humility framework can play down structural inequities. It works best paired with efforts at the system level.
Where does your organization still treat cultural competence as a finished training, and what would change if it were framed as ongoing humility?
Think of a recent interaction where a client's identity came to the front. Was it a cultural opportunity, and what happened next?
How could your team build in feedback loops so staff learn how clients actually experience them across difference?

title: Cultural Humility in Everyday Public Service
summary: Self-directed course for All staff, including supervisors and managers
body:
Cultural Humility in Everyday Public Service
Explain cultural humility as continuing attention to one’s assumptions, relationships, and public-service influence.
Receive a correction without expecting another person to teach or reassure you.
Use information about a community as preparation rather than as a personal profile.
Recognize how a routine can preserve the staff member’s interpretation after the person has challenged it.
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Cultural Humility in Everyday Public Service
Learning from another person’s meaning while examining how our assumptions and influence shape services and workplace opportunity.
Foundation self-directed learning
Knowing a service well does not mean knowing what it means to every person. Cultural humility helps you keep that distinction visible. You can draw on experience and still ask a question that changes your understanding. In this course, practice situations connect service planning, staff development, and community participation. You will consider what a response makes possible, what it may restrict, and what could happen if it becomes routine. Your own reflections can remain private, and no personal disclosure is needed.
When help carries an assumption
An offer of help can be caring and still miss what another person wants.

A person declines help. Before deciding they are reluctant, consider two meanings the refusal could have.

Which question would let their answer change your first interpretation?
Imagine offering to organize a conversation for someone and hearing that they prefer another arrangement. You may first feel that your help was rejected. The person might instead want privacy, a different pace, or control over whom they involve. None of those explanations is established yet. Notice the gap between the refusal and your interpretation. A question about what would be useful can keep the relationship open. Repeatedly treating declined help as reluctance may make a person’s choices less visible in later decisions.
What cultural humility involves
Cultural humility means continuing self-examination, openness to another person’s account, and attention to unequal influence.

Knowledge informs the question; it does not answer for the individual.

You can reconsider an assumption while keeping necessary standards and responsibilities clear.
Cultural humility is more than being modest or saying that you do not know everything. It involves examining how your learned expectations affect an exchange and whether another perspective can influence your response. A brief may explain useful history; a professional role may supply necessary expertise. Neither gives complete knowledge of the person’s priorities. Humility also leaves actual responsibilities intact. You can understand a request, explain a real limit, and explore an alternative without promising something you cannot provide.
A planning conversation to reconsider
Staff invite family because they assume family involvement is always helpful. The person requests a private conversation.

Overriding that request could leave the person’s priorities unheard. Repeating the assumption may shape plans around others’ wishes.

Ask about chosen support and the arrangement the person wants.
Here the person has supplied information that matters: they want a different arrangement. The first invitation may have been intended to help. Keeping it unchanged after the request could prevent the person from explaining something privately or choosing their own support. You do not yet know why they prefer privacy, and they need not provide a cultural biography to justify the question. Explore the request within the appropriate service arrangements. The upcoming choice asks how to respond without replacing one assumption with another.
Practice: chosen support
Staff invite family to planning. The person asks to speak privately. Staff say family involvement is usually helpful. Which response keeps the person’s wishes central?
A. Keep the invitation because the team knows what usually works.
B. Ask about the preferred arrangement and chosen support within the appropriate process.
C. Cancel planning until staff know the person’s cultural background.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The request provides evidence about the arrangement the person wants. It does not supply the reason, and you do not need to fill that gap with a cultural explanation. Compare each response by asking whether the person still has a usable opportunity to describe their priorities. Family support may be valuable when chosen; the concern is treating it as settled despite the request. Consider what repeated use of that assumption could do to planning records and future choices. Select the response that lets relevant information influence the next step while retaining the appropriate responsibilities.
Your knowledge is a starting point
Experience can help you anticipate useful questions. It can also make one explanation feel certain too soon.

Separate what the source describes from what this person has said.

Which detail could challenge the familiar explanation?
You may have learned something important from earlier service conversations. That knowledge remains useful when it prompts a thoughtful question. It becomes less reliable when it closes inquiry before the person can speak. Consider whether you are describing an observation, applying background information, or making an individual conclusion. An alternative explanation is not automatically correct either. Ask for information relevant to the current decision. This keeps learning active and prevents an old account from becoming a permanent rule for someone else.
Meaning and preference are not identical
Two people may value family while wanting different support in a particular conversation.

Ask what participation means now, rather than treating a shared value as a fixed instruction.

Circumstances and preferences can change; keep room for a later correction.
A person’s meaning may be stable in one respect and flexible in another. Family may remain important while they prefer to discuss one issue privately. An employee may value cooperation while asking for time to consider a proposal alone. You can respect the broader value without deciding that it requires the same response every time. If an earlier preference becomes the only option offered, changing circumstances may be missed. Ask about the present purpose and let the answer refine what you offer.
Influence matters in an ordinary exchange
The person arranging an agenda, recording a concern, or assigning work can make their interpretation consequential.

Being invited to speak is different from being able to influence an open choice.

Explain what can change and which limits are real.
Influence often appears through small practical decisions. The person setting a meeting agenda may decide which concerns have time to be heard. The person writing a record may determine which explanation later readers see. Cultural humility asks you to examine that position, not give up the responsibility attached to it. Make the purpose and boundaries visible. If a choice is already settled, say so honestly. Calling the conversation open while ignoring every alternative can leave participation without meaningful influence.
When someone corrects your account
A correction supplies information your first interpretation missed.

Acknowledge the specific change, revise what you can, and avoid asking the person to reassure you.

If the old account remains in a record or routine, a private change of mind may not repair its effects.
You might hear, “That is not why I asked,” or “The explanation missed what matters to me.” Take the particular correction seriously before defending the intention behind your response. You can name what you misunderstood and ask whether your revised account is accurate. Consider where the original interpretation went. If it remains in a planning note or assignment discussion, it may continue influencing later decisions. Address it through the appropriate responsibility. Acknowledging the correction is useful even when its longer-term effects remain unknown.
One way to demonstrate commitment?
A newcomer asks to send considered comments after a meeting. An experienced colleague says committed staff speak immediately.

That expectation may hide useful knowledge. If it shapes feedback, it can narrow later development opportunities.

Clarify the actual work need before treating a familiar style as the standard.
This workplace situation concerns contribution, not whether every preference can determine how a meeting operates. The team needs useful information before a decision closes. Immediate speech may be one route, but it is not automatically the only relevant evidence of commitment. Ask whether a written contribution can meet the actual need and what timing matters. If the informal style rule travels into supervision, the newcomer may receive fewer chances to demonstrate capability. The next case asks what would clarify the expectation fairly.
Practice: contribution during onboarding
A new employee offers written comments after a meeting. A colleague says committed staff speak immediately. What would clarify the expectation fairly?
A. Examine the actual work need, written contribution, and usable ways to respond.
B. Record limited commitment because the employee did not follow the usual style.
C. Assume their identity explains the preference and stop asking.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The team has a legitimate need for useful information, but the case does not establish that immediate speech is necessary to meet it. Consider the timing of the decision, the quality of the written comments, and what the newcomer was told about participation. A familiar approach may be convenient without being the only workable route. If limited speaking becomes a judgment about commitment, that judgment may affect later assignments and learning. Choose the response that checks the work and the arrangement before explaining the employee through a label.
An onboarding gap can travel forward
Unexplained expectations can make a newcomer’s contribution harder to recognize.

A judgment made early may later shape supervision, assignments, and advancement.

Check the work evidence and the introduction provided before deciding what the gap means.
An employee can know the subject and still lack insider knowledge about how a team works. If onboarding leaves that knowledge implicit, uncertainty may be mistaken for low ability or interest. The judgment may then influence assignments, reducing the experience available for later development. Trace the sequence rather than locate the whole problem inside the employee. Clarify expectations, consider actual contributions, and hear what information was missing. This does not establish that every difficulty comes from onboarding; it identifies a condition worth examining.
Respectful support includes clear limits
Listening does not require agreeing with every request or promising an unavailable option.

Explain the actual constraint and distinguish it from a preferred way of working.

A feasible alternative may preserve the purpose while improving participation.
Suppose a conversation must address a particular decision, but its usual format is flexible. You can explain the necessary purpose without treating the format as equally fixed. Ask what adjustment would help and whether it can meet that purpose. Where a request needs another responsible role, make that route clear. Cultural humility should improve the basis for responding, not replace authorized decisions. Honest limits can protect trust better than an apparent agreement followed by no meaningful change.
A brief prepares you to listen
Community briefs introduce history, institutions, and context; they do not predict an individual.

Use a brief to notice a question you might otherwise miss.

Hear current, varied perspectives without asking one person to represent everyone.
Reading beforehand can reduce the burden of beginning every conversation from zero. A brief may help you recognize histories or access conditions relevant to the issue. It cannot establish why this individual prefers an arrangement or what every person in a community would choose. Translate the background into open questions. Then listen for what fits, what differs, and what is missing. If staff repeatedly use the brief as the answer, contextual knowledge can become a profile imposed on people rather than an invitation to learn.
Partnership needs a genuine choice
A request for input should explain what people can influence and how their knowledge will be considered.

Listening without considering a relevant change may leave the same barrier in place.

Participation can be useful without assigning community members the staff’s work.
A person can contribute knowledge without taking responsibility for solving the whole service problem. Partnership respects that contribution and makes its possible influence clear. Ask a relevant question, offer usable ways to respond, and explain what happens next. If staff retain all decisions, that responsibility should be stated honestly. You can still examine how the information affects your reasoning. Repeated invitations that collect stories without considering their implications may consume people’s time while the original access barrier remains unchanged.
When a useful correction is dismissed
A participant says appointment instructions identify the building but not the entrance. Staff reply that the address is correct.

The fact is accurate, yet the route may remain unusable. Repeated dismissal favors insider knowledge.

What could the participant’s account help staff examine?
The participant is identifying a gap between an accurate address and a usable instruction. Those are different questions. Defending the address does not establish that someone can find the entrance. Ask which part of the route is unclear and consider a revision through the appropriate review. A culture brief might prepare attention to institutional experience, but the actual account identifies this practical concern. The next case asks how to use that knowledge without dismissing it or assuming it proves the same difficulty for everyone.
Practice: an instruction people can use
A participant says appointment instructions do not identify the entrance. Staff reply that the building address is correct. What would make their knowledge useful?
A. Keep the instructions because the official address is accurate.
B. Treat the account as proof that every person needs the same change.
C. Ask what was unclear, consider a usable revision, and explain what input can change.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The participant describes a practical condition that an accurate address alone does not settle. Staff know the building; a visitor may need information they take for granted. Consider how each response handles that difference. Dismissing the account can leave the entrance difficult to find. Declaring a universal solution can also overstate what one account establishes. A useful response hears the specific difficulty, explains the room for change, and considers how a revision could be reviewed. Community knowledge becomes meaningful when it can affect an appropriate open choice.
A checklist can support humility
A checklist can help make language, access, and participation questions visible.

Completing it cannot establish a person’s preferences or make an unresolved answer true.

Use the tool to support inquiry and revise the account when information changes.
Cultural humility and structured review can work together. A prompt may remind you to ask whose perspective is missing or whether a communication route is usable. That is valuable organizational support. The limitation appears when checking a box replaces hearing the person or examining the process. “Participation considered” should not conceal the fact that people could not use the invitation. Keep relevant unanswered questions visible and follow the appropriate review arrangements. The tool supports disciplined curiosity; it does not certify complete knowledge of people.
Follow the interpretation downstream
An assumption can enter a note, shape the next conversation, and become a reason to offer fewer choices.

Ask where the account is reused and who can review it.

Correcting the immediate exchange may be a beginning; recurring effects need attention to the routine.
Consider a service note that describes a person as unwilling to involve others. If their request concerned only one private conversation, the broad description could change later offers of support. The same pattern can occur when a newcomer’s meeting behavior becomes a lasting judgment about commitment. Follow where the account travels and which decisions rely on it. A correction should remain specific and respect information boundaries. This inquiry identifies a possible mechanism, not a finding that every later outcome was caused by the original note.
Ask what the response changed
A clearer explanation or revised invitation is a useful action.

Ask whether the people affected could use it and what remained difficult.

No new feedback does not prove the barrier disappeared; retain the unanswered question.
You may know that staff changed an instruction or offered a different conversation arrangement. That describes what was done. Learning about its effect requires information from the relevant experience. Ask a proportionate question: could the person identify the entrance, contribute, or understand the next step? Their account can reveal a remaining gap or a useful improvement. One response does not settle everyone’s experience. Recognizing that limit keeps follow-through thoughtful without erasing the value of a specific adjustment.
Rewrite an interpretation
Choose a practice example: “declined help,” “quiet in the meeting,” or “questioned the instruction.”

Write what was observed, one assumption to reconsider, and a question that could change it.

Then explain how leaving the assumption unchanged might affect a later choice.
Use the supplied examples so that no private records are needed. “Quiet in the meeting” is narrower than “not committed.” “Questioned the instruction” is narrower than “does not understand the service.” Select one and put the distinction into your own words. Add a question relevant to the task, then trace one possible consequence if the wider label remained. Your reflection can stay private. The purpose is to make the reasoning clearer and preserve room for evidence that does not fit the first account.
Keep the learning open
Cultural humility connects self-examination, listening, influence, and a considered response.

You can value your experience while letting another account change your interpretation.

Continue with community briefs, person-centered learning, and equity review when they help clarify the question.
You have examined why an interpretation matters and how its effects can extend beyond one exchange. Cultural humility leaves room for your experience while recognizing that another person holds knowledge you do not. A meaningful next step may be private understanding, a better question, or an appropriate change to a routine. Keep the distinction between intention and effect visible. Listen after making an adjustment, and state what remains unknown. Continued learning can deepen both relationships and the decisions through which public service takes shape.

title: Cultural Humility in Professional Judgment
summary: Self-directed course for All staff; useful for supervisors, analysts, and service partners.
body:
Cultural Humility in Professional Judgment
Use subject knowledge to ask better questions while remaining open to correction.
Identify how professional authority changes the choices available in an interaction.
Compare a familiar interpretation with the person’s explanation and relevant evidence.
Choose a practical response that preserves both participation and actual decision responsibilities.
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Cultural Humility in Professional Judgment
Using professional knowledge with curiosity, openness to correction, and attention to the people affected by a decision.
Intermediate self-directed learning
Professional knowledge helps you explain a service, examine a policy, and guide work responsibly. It does not make you the expert on every person’s experience of that work. This course explores how cultural humility can strengthen judgment rather than weaken it. You will compare familiar interpretations with new information in DSD service, workplace, and community situations. The aim is to make a decision that reflects what is known, remains honest about authority, and can change when relevant evidence reveals something important.
Expertise and the person’s experience
Staff may know a process well while someone using it sees a barrier the staff have missed.

Think of a familiar explanation. Which part depends on professional knowledge, and which part needs the person’s own account?
A process can be accurate on paper and still difficult to use. A staff member may know the correct building address, while a person trying to reach the service cannot identify the public entrance. Both accounts matter, and they answer different questions. Privately, consider an explanation you understand because of your role. Identify what a newcomer would need to know and what you could only learn by hearing their experience. This distinction keeps expertise useful without making familiarity the measure of everyone’s understanding.
What cultural humility asks of judgment
Cultural humility involves ongoing self-examination, attention to unequal power, and respectful partnership.

It keeps your understanding open to correction. It does not require abandoning expertise or agreeing to every request.
Tervalon and Murray-García described cultural humility in a historical medical education context. The concepts of ongoing reflection, power, and partnership can inform learning here without importing clinical procedures into DSD work. A humble professional examines their assumptions, asks relevant questions, and notices whose knowledge can shape the interaction. That approach preserves responsibility for accurate information. It also recognizes that professional experience may not reveal how another person encounters the same process, or what a seemingly small detail means in daily life.
A correct address and an unclear entrance
Staff provide the correct address. A person says the entrance is difficult to find. The response is, “The directions are complete.”

Examining the actual route could reveal missing information and prevent a familiar process from remaining difficult to use.
Imagine that staff have checked a letter against the official address and see no error. The person’s concern is different: several entrances are visible, and the public one is not identified. Calling the directions complete dismisses information the person is in a position to know. The more useful response examines the particular gap and prepares an accurate clarification through the appropriate responsibility. The concern may reveal a barrier, but we do not yet know how many people encounter it or whether another change is needed.
Practice: the correct address
A person says the public entrance is difficult to find. Staff have checked that the address is correct. What response best reflects cultural humility in professional judgment?
A. Hear the specific difficulty, examine the route, and prepare an accurate clarification appropriately.
B. Repeat the address because the professional information has already been checked.
C. Ask the person to explain their cultural background before considering the concern.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
This situation gives staff accurate information and a person a relevant experience. The professional account does not have to be wrong for the experience to reveal a gap. The concern is about recognizing the entrance, while the checked information concerns the address. Consider which response allows the question to become more precise and supports an appropriate clarification. Then examine the possible repeated effect if unclear routes are always described as complete: people with insider knowledge may obtain access more easily than those encountering the process for the first time.
The meaning behind your first reaction
A professional may associate a familiar process with fairness, consistency, or reliability. Another person may experience the same process differently.

Examine why the first interpretation feels convincing before making it the only explanation.
Consistency often matters in public service. That value may make an unchanged instruction feel fair because everyone receives the same words. Yet equal wording does not establish equal access to the knowledge needed to use it. Examining this reaction does not require rejecting consistency. It asks whether the instruction’s purpose is being met. You can value reliable information while recognizing a missing explanation. Cultural humility makes room for that reconsideration without treating your earlier understanding as evidence that you are a bad person.
What you know and what you inferred
“The form was not returned” is an observation. “The person is not interested” adds a reason.

A useful judgment separates the facts, possible explanations, and information needed to choose a response.
An incomplete step may have several explanations: misunderstanding, a practical barrier, disagreement, changed plans, or something else. Some may be more plausible in the circumstances, but the observation alone does not decide. Professional judgment uses relevant evidence to distinguish them. It should not make unlimited demands for personal information. Ask what would help understand the actual task and respond within your responsibility. The person may correct your account, explain a difficulty, or make a choice you did not expect.
Curiosity with a relevant purpose
Ask about the information or experience needed for the decision. Avoid making personal disclosure the price of being heard.

“What part is difficult to use?” can reveal more than “Why are people from your community reluctant?”
Professional curiosity is strongest when it has a clear purpose. A relevant question can help locate a missing step, understand a concern, or distinguish a real requirement from a habit. A question about someone’s entire cultural history may be interesting to staff but unnecessary for the task. Invite the person’s account without assigning a group explanation. Some information may be required by an authorized process; explain that honestly. Optional reflection should never disguise a requirement or create an extra condition for consideration.
Listening and influence
A person can be heard without having any influence over the next step. Explain what their contribution can shape.

Consider whether the response changes an explanation, an option, a recommendation, or nothing that remains open.
Listening is valuable, but it is not the same as sharing influence. A professional may summarize a person’s concern accurately and still continue with a preferred approach without examining it. Sometimes a real requirement limits the available choices. Explain that limit and consider what can still change. Perhaps the wording, contact method, or timing within the actual process is open. Being honest about those choices respects the person’s contribution more than suggesting that everything is negotiable when it is not.
Ideas after the answer is announced
A supervisor announces a development plan, then asks an employee for ideas. The employee cannot tell what is still open.

Clarifying the real choices makes participation more meaningful and may reveal a concern the supervisor had not considered.
In a development conversation, the supervisor may already have decided an assignment’s purpose while its support arrangements remain open. The employee needs to understand that distinction. A vague invitation can encourage agreement while making a different view feel unwelcome. A clearer explanation identifies the available choices and invites relevant questions. If decisions repeatedly close before employees can contribute, useful knowledge about workload, preparation, or access may be missed. Examine the actual opportunities and responses before concluding that an invitation created shared influence.
Practice: input after a decision
A supervisor announces an assignment and then asks the employee for ideas. The employee is unsure what can change. Which response would make participation more meaningful?
A. Assure the employee that all input is welcome without discussing the decision’s limits.
B. Explain what is decided, what remains open, and how relevant concerns can affect the next step.
C. Assume that silence means the employee respects the supervisor’s authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
Professional authority changes the choices available in a conversation. The supervisor may have a legitimate responsibility to decide an assignment, but the employee needs to know whether the purpose, timing, support, or some other part remains open. Consider which response describes that reality honestly. A vague invitation can sound inclusive while leaving the employee unsure whether a concern will matter. If this happens repeatedly, relevant knowledge about preparation or access may never shape development decisions. The case asks you to improve participation without pretending that all authority is shared.
Authority and expectations of respect
People may differ in how they understand respectful participation around authority. A question, a pause, or a gentle concern can carry different meanings.

Clarify the opportunity to contribute without ranking people by deference or confidence.
Expectations about authority can influence when and how a person speaks. Someone may wait for a clear invitation because that signals respect; another may ask a question promptly for the same reason. These possibilities are not fixed traits or national categories. In the workplace, explain who decides and how relevant input can be raised. Avoid treating confidence as proof of competence or waiting as proof of agreement. The purpose is to understand the exchange and provide a usable opportunity to contribute, while keeping real responsibilities clear.
Requirements and avoidable habits
Identify the actual requirement and the choices available within it. A customary practice is not automatically a necessary condition.

Explore an alternative without promising a change that you cannot authorize.
A service or workplace process may contain both a real requirement and habits that grew around it. For example, an instruction may need to identify a particular next step, while its reliance on insider terminology is avoidable. Professional humility asks you to examine that distinction rather than defend every familiar detail as necessary. Any proposed change still follows the appropriate responsibility and review. A person’s concern may justify looking again, but it does not automatically establish which alternative is accurate, feasible, or authorized.
Community knowledge that adds to the question
Community participants can identify experiences that staff have not seen. Different accounts may reveal different barriers or priorities.

Hear the specific knowledge offered. No participant should have to represent an entire community.
Community engagement can change the question itself. Staff may ask whether an instruction is accurate; participants may ask whether it makes the response understandable or reachable. Both concerns can belong in the analysis. Respectful partnership means explaining how input can shape the work and being open to a perspective that differs from the familiar one. A person’s account is not universal proof, but it is also not irrelevant because it comes from experience rather than professional training. Examine its relevance to the decision.
Culture briefs as preparation
A culture brief can suggest questions about relationships, communication, and experience. It cannot supply an individual’s answer.

Use it to prepare respectfully, then listen for differences within and across communities.
A brief is most useful when it reminds you that familiar expectations may not be shared. It can suggest a question about how people receive information or understand participation. It becomes less useful when treated as a profile that explains everyone. In engagement, people may agree with part of a brief, reject another part, or raise a concern outside it. Let that information change your understanding. Also notice which perspectives remain absent because the invitation, format, or access arrangements limit participation.
A service proposal challenged by lived experience
A team prefers an online explanation. Participants say the proposal assumes access and knowledge some people may not have.

Examine the concern, the evidence, and feasible alternatives. Agreement with staff is not the test of useful participation.
The preferred proposal may have practical strengths and still rely on an assumption that needs examination. Hearing an access concern does not mean accepting every suggested alternative immediately. It means asking what evidence supports the concern and how the proposal could respond. Staff should explain the choices that remain open and what will inform the recommendation. If familiar professional reasoning always outweighs experience without examination, engagement may appear inclusive while leaving important barriers untouched. The task is to improve the analysis, not obtain approval for a settled answer.
Practice: a preferred service proposal
Community participants say a preferred online explanation may not be usable for everyone. Staff believe the proposal is efficient. What response would best improve the judgment?
A. Retain the proposal because professional experience is the strongest form of knowledge.
B. Adopt every suggested alternative immediately to show that community voices matter.
C. Examine the access concern and evidence, explain the open choices, and compare feasible responses.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
The disagreement concerns which evidence belongs in the judgment. Staff know the process and its practical demands; participants describe possible difficulties using the proposed explanation. Those perspectives may reveal both strengths and gaps. Consider which response can examine the access question without demanding agreement with staff or making promises before alternatives are understood. Culture briefs may help prepare questions about communication, but they cannot establish everyone’s access to an online explanation. The analysis needs relevant accounts, actual requirements, and clear information about the choices that remain open.
When expertise becomes the only accepted knowledge
If only professional explanations count, missing perspectives may remain outside service and workplace decisions.

Repeated dismissal can preserve barriers. Examine how contributions affected the question and the eventual response.
Expertise becomes restrictive when it is used to decide in advance that other knowledge cannot matter. A service user may identify a difficult step. An employee may describe an assignment barrier. A community participant may question an access assumption. Repeatedly dismissing those accounts can preserve routines that work better for people with familiar information or influence. That is a mechanism to investigate, rather than a finding established by one disagreement. Examine the contribution, the response, and whether relevant information entered the decision.
A judgment that can be examined
Compare relevant records, different accounts, actual choices, and consequences. Include information that could challenge your first view.

The number of invitations or comments alone does not show that people had meaningful influence.
To examine a concern about participation, look beyond whether a meeting occurred. What did people have enough information to discuss? Which options were genuinely open? How was their contribution addressed? A record of those questions can help distinguish an invitation from actual influence. Handle information through the appropriate work arrangements and avoid collecting sensitive stories simply to demonstrate thoroughness. Evidence may support an adjustment, reveal another issue, or leave an important uncertainty. A responsible judgment states those limits rather than filling them with confidence.
Humility across the employee life cycle
Recruitment, onboarding, supervision, development, and retention all involve assumptions about what employees know and need.

Ask whether staff can question an expectation and whether relevant experience can change the response.
A hiring process may assume that applicants know government language. Onboarding may treat questions as lack of preparation. Supervision may close a discussion before hearing an access concern. Development may favor people with familiar networks. These examples connect humility to different points in an employee’s experience without assuming one cause explains them all. The shared practice is to examine professional assumptions and hear relevant information. A supervisor can remain responsible for decisions while explaining them accurately and considering information that challenges a preferred approach.
Reconsidering a professional explanation
Privately rewrite: “The process is clear; the person must not understand it.” Separate your knowledge from the person’s experience.

Identify a relevant question, a possible response, and what evidence would still be needed.
Imagine a person tells you that the next step is unclear even though you know the process well. Rewrite the judgment so it leaves room for information you may have missed. Ask what the explanation assumes and what a relevant question could establish. Then choose a possible response within the actual responsibility. This exercise does not require a personal account or a new staff assignment. Its value is in examining your reasoning and understanding how another perspective could change the explanation, while keeping unresolved questions visible.
Professional knowledge that remains open
Use expertise to explain accurately and ask better questions. Remain open to relevant correction.

Describe real choices and responsibilities.

Examine whose knowledge influences decisions, and how repeated routines may preserve or reduce barriers.
Cultural humility strengthens judgment when it connects openness with a responsible response. You can know a process well, explain its actual requirements, and still learn something important from another person’s experience. Across DSD services, workplace culture, and community engagement, that combination can reveal barriers a familiar explanation missed. Consider what you would now question in a decision, whose perspective would help, and what remains unknown. The next useful response should follow the evidence and the actual responsibility, rather than defend familiarity for its own sake.

title: Both are true
summary: Learning about a community does not establish what an individual wants. Following a structured process does not remove the need for that conversation.
body:
Learning about a community does not establish what an individual wants. Following a structured process does not remove the need for that conversation.

A useful review combines questions about the person’s experience with questions about the organization’s process.

Cultural humility starts with recognizing that your interpretation may be incomplete. A brief can help you prepare for a conversation, but the person receiving services remains the source of their own priorities and preferences. Asking a question matters only if the answer can influence what you understand or do next.

Structured analysis addresses a different responsibility: explaining how a decision was developed, whose experience informed it, and what benefits or burdens were considered. A team can complete every field yet overlook an important perspective. It can also express curiosity without following through on a concern. Use the applicable agency process while asking what the available information leaves unresolved; neither a completed form nor a considerate conversation establishes that the resulting service is accessible.

Check your understanding

A worker refuses the toolkit because “humility isn’t a form.” What is the strongest read?

Option 1: Skip the Equity Analysis Toolkit because using a form is incompatible with cultural humility.

Option 2: Use the relevant analysis tool while asking the people affected what the available information misses.

Option 3: Use only NCCC checklists, regardless of the decision or applicable DHS process.

Option 4: Avoid all forms and documentation when working across cultural differences.

Answer review

Correct response: Use the relevant analysis tool while asking the people affected what the available information misses.

Feedback for the correct response

Correct. Effective practice requires balancing humility toward people with structured methods that clarify and document the decision process.

Feedback for another response

Cultural humility does not replace an applicable agency requirement. Identify the process that governs the decision, and use inquiry to improve the information considered within it.

Put this lesson to work

Within your responsibility

Determine your area of influence within this process. Identify collaborators and gather the supporting information that will inform a responsible next action.

What could go wrong

A team can complete learning or documentation while leaving the concern that prompted the review unresolved.

A next step

If useful to your work, compare a completed review with the question that prompted it. Explain what the evidence supports and what still needs to be asked; a completed form alone does not settle the concern.

Learning objective

Identify the practical implication of “Both are true” and apply it to one live DHS decision connected to Cultural Humility vs. a Checklist.

Key points

A fact sheet is not a person. A blank analysis is not humility.

Reflect on how this principle may affect a decision you participate in. Research the specific data and obligations connected to that situation before taking further steps.

If this is relevant to your work, choose a manageable next step with the responsible person. Agree what you will check and when you will return to it.

Practice and reflection

Use the practice decision to explain your reasoning. You may keep a private note about a next step; no personal reflection needs to be submitted.

If useful to your work, compare a completed review with the question that prompted it. Explain what the evidence supports and what still needs to be asked; a completed form alone does not settle the concern.

Practice situation

A team is considering how to apply this lesson to its work. Someone wants to label which employees or community members understand the idea before the work decision itself has been examined.

How should the team use the concept?

Option 1: Use it to identify who needs more development before they can participate.

Response to this choice

The program does not turn a reflection map or learning concept into a character score or gate to participation.

Option 2: Avoid the concept entirely because disagreement could be uncomfortable.

Response to this choice

Avoidance leaves the existing default untouched. The safer object of analysis is the work, not the worth of the people in the room.

Option 3 — recommended response: Use the concept to examine the work, check what is known and uncertain, and agree a responsible next step.

Response to this choice

This uses the concept to improve inquiry without ranking people. Evidence may support retaining a sound practice, revising it, or referring an unresolved question; a change is not automatically the right result.

Applying the learning

How could you apply this lesson to a practice example or an appropriate work question?

Apply this lesson to one current piece of work connected to Cultural Humility vs. a Checklist.

Describe affected roles or groups without names, the question to resolve, and the role that can consider a proportionate response.

Use the right-door guide if a formal duty or accountable office may be involved.

Sources

Georgetown’s National Center for Cultural Competence provides organizational self-assessment resources. Use the relevant tool’s guidance and examine supporting evidence; this course does not turn a checklist into a rating of a person.

(https://nccc.georgetown.edu/)

DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit (this hub)

Related program learning on the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. Check the current agency process and the scope of the decision rather than treating this course as the official procedure.

Related program learning on cultural brokering as a role. Use it to examine when contextual knowledge or communication support may help, while still asking the person about their own priorities.

title: The limits of a fact sheet
summary: A claim about “how Hmong families are” turns background information into a stereotype. Ask what matters to the particular person or family.
body:
A claim about “how Hmong families are” turns background information into a stereotype. Ask what matters to the particular person or family.

A community brief can introduce history, language, and experiences with institutions that staff might otherwise overlook. Its value is to improve preparation and questions, not to supply answers on another person’s behalf. A description drawn from one study or setting also needs its limitations kept visible when you use it in Minnesota human services.

For example, a service worker may read that some families value involvement in planning. That does not establish whom a particular person wants involved, what information they wish to share, or whether the available meeting arrangements work. Ask the person about those choices, arrange the communication support they need, and revisit your interpretation when their answer differs from your expectation. Community knowledge and individual self-determination belong in the same conversation.

Applying the lesson

Within your responsibility

Identify which interpretation is yours and which preference the person has actually expressed. Ask a question that could distinguish them.

What could go wrong

A general statement from a brief becomes a service recommendation without checking whether it fits the person’s circumstances or wishes.

A next step

Ask whom the person wants involved and what support would make participation useful. Explain which arrangements you can change and which need another role.

Learning objective

Explain how the limitations of fact sheets influence decision-making in DHS work, and apply this reasoning to one active service, form, policy, or process where individual engagement is essential.

Key points

A brief about a group or culture cannot substitute for learning about the actual person. Engage directly with the individual or family your work affects.

Consider how relying solely on summaries or general guides could influence a decision in your assigned responsibilities. Review all relevant specifics and roles before taking action.

If applicable, select a practical, actionable next step within your authority. Coordinate with the responsible person to define what you will assess and set an agreed timeline for follow-up.

Practice and reflection

Use the practice decision to explain your reasoning. You may keep a private note about a next step; no personal reflection needs to be submitted.

If useful to your work, use a cultural brief to prepare an open question. Explain how you would check your interpretation with the person instead of predicting a preference from group membership.

A team is considering how to apply this lesson to its work. Someone wants to label which employees or community members understand the idea before the work decision itself has been examined.

How should the team use the concept?

title: When a checklist is the right tool
summary: An organizational checklist can direct attention to policies, resources, and service conditions. Its usefulness depends on the evidence behind each response.
body:
An organizational checklist can direct attention to policies, resources, and service conditions. Its usefulness depends on the evidence behind each response.

Use a checklist to examine the system

Toolkit

The Equity Analysis Toolkit supports a structured examination of a decision, including affected people, relevant information, benefits, burdens, and follow-through. Follow the applicable DHS process for the decision in front of you. Completing a learning activity does not itself complete that process or establish that a proposed change has been approved.

CLAS or language plan

A language-access checklist may ask whether people are informed about interpreter services. A checked box should lead to a concrete explanation of how that information is provided and whether the person can use the service. Notification alone does not demonstrate that interpretation was available, timely, or useful in the encounter.

NCCC organizational checklist

NCCC organizational checklists support reflection on conditions such as policies, budgets, and training. Use the responses to identify evidence and questions for further inquiry. The checklist does not establish an individual employee’s competence or prove that people experience equitable access.

Practice: Apply this lesson

Within your responsibility

Identify where you can take action within your current work. Determine who must be involved and what information or policy details will inform a sound next step.

What could go wrong

The team records that interpretation is available without checking whether people know how to request it or can use it when needed.

A next step

Choose one checklist response and identify the information supporting it. Discuss any gap with the role responsible for the service condition.

Learning objective

Recognize when a checklist or structured tool is necessary and apply this understanding to a real DHS process or decision connected to Cultural Humility vs. a Checklist.

Key points

A checklist identifies questions to examine. The evidence and follow-through determine what the organization can reasonably conclude.

Consider how structured tools clarify information and responsibilities relevant to a DHS decision. Review requirements and intended outcomes before acting.

If this approach applies, select a realistic action item, confirm roles and responsibilities, and set clear milestones for review with the appropriate person.

Practice and reflection

Use the practice decision to explain your reasoning. You may keep a private note about a next step; no personal reflection needs to be submitted.

For optional practice, examine one checklist response. Distinguish an arrangement, such as an interpreter contract, from evidence that people can obtain the support. Identify a proportionate follow-up with the responsible role.

Practice situation

In a practice service review, a team marks interpreter services as available because a contract is in place. Staff have not checked how people learn about the service, how requests are arranged, or what happens when an interpreter is unavailable.

What should the team do with this checklist response?

Option 1: Treat the contract as sufficient evidence that everyone can use interpreter services.

Response to this choice

A contract establishes an arrangement, not the experience of obtaining support. The team still needs to understand how the service works in practice.

Option 2: Stop using the checklist because a checked box cannot prove an outcome.

Response to this choice

The checklist can still identify a useful question. The limitation calls for evidence and follow-up, rather than abandoning structured review.

Option 3 — recommended response: Keep the contract information, identify the unanswered access questions, and ask the responsible roles how those conditions are checked.

Response to this choice

This preserves what is known while making the evidence gap visible. The next step examines information, requests, and actual availability without assuming that a checked box establishes access.

body:
Turn a useful question into a responsible next step. Explain what can change, who can act, and how the person will learn what happened.

Apply this

1. Choose a practice example or a work issue that can be discussed without identifying a service recipient or colleague. What assumption could the team check?

2. Write a question that invites the person’s own priorities without suggesting the answer. What response would cause the team to reconsider its approach?

3. Identify the decision and the applicable review process. What information is still needed, and which role can act on it?

4. Choose a proportionate way to follow up. How will the team distinguish completing an activity from improving the person’s opportunity to use a service?

Apply this lesson

Within your responsibility

Determine your area of influence for this decision, who should be consulted or included in the process, and what information is needed to guide the next step.

What could go wrong

The person describes a barrier, but the team records only that engagement occurred and gives no explanation of the next step.

A next step

Summarize the concern without identifying personal details, confirm the responsible role, and explain how a response will be communicated.

Learning objective

Explain how a question, an accountable next step, and a response to participants can connect cultural humility to a DHS decision.

Key points

A community summary may improve your ability to ask purposeful questions, but individual experiences always inform what is appropriate in practice.

Identify a feasible action step for your role and outline which factors or information you would verify before implementing or describing a procedural change.

Practice and reflection

Use the practice decision to explain your reasoning. You may keep a private note about a next step; no personal reflection needs to be submitted.

For optional practice, outline how a team could report back on a concern. State what was heard, what can be considered, who can respond, and how participants would learn the outcome.

During a practice review, community participants explain that a response process is difficult to use. The team records that engagement occurred, but the summary does not retain the concern or identify who will respond. Participants receive a thank-you message with no explanation of the next step.

What follow-through would make the engagement more useful?

Option 1: Count the meeting as completed and close the issue because participants had an opportunity to speak.

Response to this choice

An opportunity to speak does not show that the concern informed the decision. Closing the issue would leave the response barrier and responsibility unresolved.

Option 2: Promise that every requested change will be implemented before checking authority or feasibility.

Response to this choice

A promise beyond the team’s authority can undermine trust. Meaningful follow-through requires an honest account of what can change and what needs further review.

Option 3 — recommended response: Confirm the concern, identify the role that can respond, and explain what will be considered and how participants will hear back.

Response to this choice

This connects the contribution to a decision and a responsible next step. It allows the team to explain both changes and constraints without treating acknowledgement as resolution.
